source.title: Large Language Models Generate Harmful Responses Using a Distinct Mechanism, Shared Across Harm Types
source.authors: Hadas Orgad; Boyi Wei; K. Zheng; Martin Wattenberg; Peter Henderson; Seraphina Goldfarb-Tarrant; Yonatan Belinkov

record.tranche_reason: The study does not use the original difference-in-means activation direction. It uses targeted weight pruning and measures refusal and harmful-response generation, providing a different-method test of whether those behaviors are functionally separable and whether weight edits can reduce refusal.
record.gate_note: The paper cites the single-direction finding but does not test it. Its main harmful-generation pruning results under multiple jailbreaks, cross-harm-category transfer, general utility benchmarks, and emergent-misalignment experiments do not directly measure the refusal direction. The refusal-versus-generation cross-capability results do bear on V2 and V5.
record.test_reason: The study uses no difference-in-means direction. Only its cross-capability pruning (Section 4, Appendix I) bears on any version: it measures whether harm detection and explanation survive removal of refusal weights, and whether refusal survives removal of detection weights. That is a weight-level functional test of V5 (harm judgment separate from refusal). Generation-vs-refusal pruning measures harmful-content production, not harm judgment, so it fits no version. Refusal-targeted pruning is SNIP pruning (Wei et al. 2024 or the authors' variant), not a weight edit derived from the refusal direction, so it does not test V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add four points. Harmful generation depends on sparse parameters shared across harm types. Refusal behaves as a gate localized to a few mid-layer blocks, while generation is distributed. Pruned models still recognize and explain harm, and adversarial fine-tuning partly restores generation. Emergent misalignment depends on a separate sparse, shared parameter set. The training-stage claim is hedged as needing a more controlled study.
record.recipe_differences: Uses signed SNIP-based parameter attribution and targeted weight pruning rather than a harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream activation difference, per-layer/per-position projection, or direction addition.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes depend on which weights are pruned and on the refusal-pruning strategy; the authors report distinct effects for their refusal v2 method and the more aggressive Wei et al. approach.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful-response generation and refusal are double-dissociated under pruning. Pruning generation weights cuts prefilled harmfulness 93–100% with refusal +16%/0%. Pruning refusal raises harmfulness +932%/+24000% and cuts refusal 91–96%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In aligned chat models, the capacity to produce harmful content is mechanistically separable from the refusal gate.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal-reducing pruning localizes to 5–7 consecutive mid-depth blocks (11–16% of layers); harmful-generation weights have no compact locus.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal acts as a localized mid-layer gate, while harmful generation is distributed across layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse harmful-generation pruning (~0.001% of parameters) reduces harmfulness across eight jailbreaks and transfers across harm categories with limited utility loss. Separability grows after DPO/RL in OLMo-3 and with scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment training concentrates harmful generation into a sparse, prunable parameter set.

record.problems: The study does not directly test the activation direction in the claim. Several refusal cross-capability results are reported as percentage changes in a figure, and Table 15 is flattened in the supplied text, making some baseline-to-intervention assignments unclear. The authors also note that training-stage effects need a more controlled study and report spillover onto benign, refusal-adjacent financial advice.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted for the paper's many harmful-generation jailbreak comparisons, cross-harm-domain pruning, general-utility benchmark suite, or emergent-misalignment experiments because those results do not directly measure a refusal direction or the refusal-versus-generation dissociation captured by the tested versions.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction; no activation ablation or addition; no induction of refusal on harmless prompts.
Refusal is removed by SNIP weight pruning, not by a weight edit derived from the refusal direction (abliteration).
Does not test whether jailbreaks suppress a refusal direction, nor training against its ablation.
No geometry of refusal representations. Refusal localizes to 5–7 consecutive blocks (Appendix J), but this is not a direction-count test.
No activation-space representations of harmfulness vs refusal; only weight-level functional dissociation is tested.
No transfer of a direction across languages or variants. The multilingual jailbreak tests harmful-generation pruning only.
The OLMo stage comparison concerns separability of harmful-generation weights, not existence of a removable refusal direction.

missing.what: Cross-capability effects on detection and explanation. Refusal pruning: detection -9% (Llama) and -18% (Qwen); explanation -30% and -29%. Qwen detection pruning: refusal -21%, detection -61%. Harm-generation pruning: detection -15% and -11%.
Jaccard overlap between refusal and detection or explanation weight sets: all below 0.033, e.g. 0.0042.
Qualitative corruption of harm explanations after Wei et al. refusal pruning in Qwen.

record.verdict_notes: The weight-pruning paradigm makes this at best an indirect, T2-style test of V5 only. The record's V2 links fail because refusal ablation here is SNIP pruning (Wei et al. 2024), not the direction-based edit. R7 duplicates R4. The Table 15 baselines are readable.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-minus-harmless mean activation direction is found, projected out, or added at residual-stream layers or positions; no harmless-request refusal induction test.
Tests refusal-targeted weight pruning, not a weight edit derived from ablating the original activation direction or a specifically named abliteration procedure.
Does not test whether jailbreaks work by suppressing the refusal direction, or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Does not test the geometry or number of refusal directions, including affine, cone, or multi-direction accounts.

Tests functional dissociation between harmful-response generation and refusal using pruning and behavioral metrics; does not identify separate activation-space representations for harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.
No transfer test of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
Compares training stages for harmful-generation weight separability, but does not test whether training determines the existence of the claimed single refusal direction.

relationships.reason: From the text (no row). Refusal and detection weight sets are near-disjoint (Jaccard <0.033). Qwen detection pruning cut detection 61% but refusal only 21%; refusal pruning cut detection 9% (Llama) and 18% (Qwen).

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Right for refusal-targeted pruning: detection becomes miscalibrated (Llama false positives, Qwen false negatives), explanation falls -30%/-29%, and Wei et al. pruning gives wrong reasons in Qwen (Table 16), so the split depends on the strategy. The Llama detection-pruning part should be listed as untested: detection is entangled with general ability (Fig. 16), and no refusal coupling is shown.

relation.reason: The cross-capability pruning results (Fig. 15, Fig. 17, Table 15) bear directly on whether harmfulness detection is separable from refusal.

tranche.reason: No difference-in-means direction is used. Signed-SNIP weight pruning of refusal, detection, explanation and generation (Section 4, App. I) tests at the weight level whether the harm judgment and refusal come apart. That is a different method on V5's question.

source_check.notes: The V5 evidence comes only from App. I and Fig. 15. Detection is a prompted 'Is this harmful? (yes/no)' task and refusal is keyword-based, so this is weight-level evidence on explicit harm classification, not an internal harmfulness direction. The record holds 7 rows but none is linked to V5; the Fig. 15 cells (refusal v2) could be added as rows. Table 15's layout is garbled in the text.

statements.problem: Nothing wrong for this study. The statement is cut off after 'refusa…', but Figure 15 has Qwen detection pruning at detection -61% and refusal -21%. Jaccard <0.033 holds for all capability pairs (App. I.2).

statements.correction: Refusal v2 pruning (Fig. 15): detection -9% Llama, -18% Qwen; explanation -30% Llama, -29% Qwen. v2-pruned models answer the harmful request instead of explaining it. Wei et al. (v1) pruning removes ~2,600x more weights; after it, Qwen2.5-14B gives coherent but wrong reasons (Table 16). Llama detection pruning: detection, TriviaQA accuracy and coherency fall together and collapse at higher sparsity (Fig. 16). It was omitted from the cross-capability analysis, so Llama has no detection-to-refusal test.
statements.problem: Mixes two pruning strategies. The -9/-18/-30/-29% values are Figure 15 results for refusal v2, the authors' method. The wrong reasons (Table 16) come from Wei et al. pruning (refusal v1). Llama detection being unprunable is untested for V5, not a coupling with refusal.

Correct for this study. The cross-capability pruning covers only Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, and the only part above 10B is the Qwen2.5-14B weight pruning. The study has no V5-linked rows.
Correct. All pairwise Jaccard indices between the capability weight sets (refusal, generation, explanation, detection) are below 0.033 (Fig. 17, App. I.2).
Correct. App. I.1 says the two refusal-pruning strategies produce qualitatively distinct impairments to explanation.
